records.label: The Stop-Hook Loop
records.summary: Use a stop hook to inspect an agent's proposed exit and decide whether the current task has eligible next work. The hook consults durable state, evidence and remaining budget; it can allow a stop, return a bounded diagnostic or require escalation. Re-entry continues the same contract and accounting rather than granting a fresh objective or unlimited retries.
records.limitation: A stop hook is only an integration point; its presence does not prove that all exits, subprocesses or tool effects are controlled.

attributes.label: The Stop-Hook Loop
attributes.required_revision: Treat a stop hook as a variant; re-entry must not erase budgets or permit changing the oracle.
attributes.limitation: A stop hook is only an integration point; its presence does not prove that all exits, subprocesses or tool effects are controlled.

practice.purpose: Avoid premature completion claims while retaining an explicit way to stop when further autonomous work is unjustified.
when_to_use: An existing agent runtime provides a reliable exit callback and the task has machine-checkable completion prerequisites.
A bounded diagnostic can legitimately guide one more attempt under the same objective.
when_not_to_use: The hook rejects every stop until the agent asserts success more convincingly.
A missing owner decision or permission is being treated as something another generation attempt can resolve.
prerequisites: An understood runtime hook contract and a durable task ledger.
Protected expectations plus explicit retry, hold, cancellation and review-readiness outcomes.
steps: Define which evidence must be present for the proposed exit and which gaps require an owner rather than another attempt.
At the hook, read the exact candidate state and cumulative budget instead of relying on a prose completion summary.
If an in-scope diagnostic remains and budget permits, return one bounded instruction identifying the failed obligation.
Preserve the same contract and oracle on re-entry, recording the hook decision and charging all work to the existing task.
Allow a typed stop for exhaustion, cancellation, unclear intention or unavailable authority, retaining the unfinished obligations for handoff.
practice.example: Illustrative example: An agent proposes to stop after changing a replay function. The hook finds that its required independent replay result is missing and requests that check within the remaining budget. The check reveals an unresolved policy question, so the next hook decision is a hold for the policy owner. It does not force the agent to rewrite the expected result until the exit appears green.
verification: Each re-entry has a recorded diagnostic, eligibility decision and remaining allowance.
Cancellation and exhausted-budget exits are possible even when the task is incomplete.
The hook cannot modify protected expectations or convert a review-ready state into acceptance.
outputs: Hook decision log and persistent continuation state.
Current candidate evidence or a clear hold with the required owner decision.
risks: Repeated automatic re-entry can conceal a loop with no new information.
A runtime-specific hook may miss alternate termination paths unless those paths are explicitly tested.

records.label: The Editor-Native Manual Loop
records.summary: Use a human-guided editor session as a complete and legitimate execution route: select one scoped action, inspect its result, obtain relevant evidence and decide what happens next. The engineer controls progression while the assistant contributes drafts, explanations or diagnostics. Manual guidance is suitable when its observed overhead is lower than maintaining an additional autonomous controller.
records.limitation: Human presence does not guarantee correct review or safe tool use; the session still needs appropriate scope, evidence and decision rights.

attributes.label: The Editor-Native Manual Loop
attributes.required_revision: A manually guided session is a legitimate alternative, not a compulsory lower stage of maturity.
attributes.limitation: Human presence does not guarantee correct review or safe tool use; the session still needs appropriate scope, evidence and decision rights.

practice.purpose: Keep simple or judgment-heavy changes manageable without adding coordination machinery that does not resolve a concrete uncertainty.
when_to_use: A small change has a clear diff and a direct verification step.
Frequent interpretation decisions make interactive guidance useful and affordable.
when_not_to_use: A long task loses critical state whenever the editor session closes.
The engineer is expected to rubber-stamp every tool action without inspecting the consequential decisions.
prerequisites: A clear authorized objective and the existing repository permission boundaries.
A practical way to inspect the diff, run relevant checks and retain the final decision.
steps: Choose the next meaningful increment and identify what the assistant may inspect or change.
Ask for a candidate or diagnostic with its assumptions visible, keeping the approved behavior separate from the proposed implementation.
Inspect the changed code or artifact and run the check appropriate to its actual consequence.
Use the observation to continue, revise the approach or stop for clarification; do not repeat suggestions without a new reason.
Retain a short record of the final revision, evidence, unresolved issues and responsible acceptance decision.
practice.example: Illustrative example: A maintainer corrects a non-authoritative help heading with assistance in the editor. They inspect the one-file diff and render the page to confirm its appearance and links. No parallel coordinator is needed. If the edit unexpectedly changes executable routing text, they pause to clarify the newly affected behavior instead of assuming the same lightweight route remains adequate.
verification: The final diff stays within the agreed scope or records an authorized change to it.
The check answers the actual obligation, such as rendered wording or runtime behavior, rather than merely confirming that the file saved.
The maintainer can explain the result and what would require a stronger review route.
outputs: Scoped candidate with proportionate verification evidence.
Short decision record and any trigger for reconsidering the execution route.
risks: Interactive convenience can make unrecorded assumptions difficult to recover later.
A confident human can still accept a plausible generated change without checking its consequential behavior.

records.label: Run Until Done: Retry Against Reality
records.summary: Retry a bounded task only when a concrete observation provides a reason to expect the next attempt to address an identified failure. Preserve the authorized objective and protected expectations, record the attempted remedy and recheck the candidate. Done means reaching the appropriate reviewed state or a named stop, not an assumption that enough retries must eventually converge.
records.limitation: Repeated attempts can remain correlated, consume budget or introduce new defects; neither a loop nor a model change guarantees convergence to an acceptable result.

attributes.label: Run Until Done: Retry Against Reality
attributes.required_revision: Retry only against a verifiable diagnosis with a stopping rule; convergence is not guaranteed.
attributes.limitation: Repeated attempts can remain correlated, consume budget or introduce new defects; neither a loop nor a model change guarantees convergence to an acceptable result.

practice.purpose: Replace indefinite regeneration with a sequence of explainable repairs whose eligibility can be checked by someone outside the maker.
when_to_use: A test, reproduction or concrete review finding identifies an in-scope defect.
The next attempt has a plausible targeted remedy and sufficient remaining budget.
when_not_to_use: The only feedback is that the answer is unsatisfactory, with no actionable observation.
The disagreement concerns intended behavior, unavailable authority or a prohibited operation.
prerequisites: A persistent task and attempt record with explicit budgets and exits.
An oracle or other evidence source that the maker cannot rewrite to achieve a pass.
steps: Capture the failed obligation, exact candidate, diagnostic and relevant environment before proposing another attempt.
Decide whether the failure is repairable within the current contract or needs a named owner to clarify scope.
State the narrow change expected to address the diagnostic and check that it is permitted and affordable.
Apply the repair, rerun the protected check and examine relevant regressions for unintended effects.
Continue only if new evidence supports another eligible attempt; otherwise retain the history and stop as review-ready, exhausted, blocked or escalated.
practice.example: Illustrative example: A checker shows that a revised export drops one allowed status value. The maker corrects that mapping and reruns the status cases. The next review raises an unresolved question about whether that status should exist for a different customer class. This is no longer a mechanical retry: the task stops for a requirement decision, preserving the previous failure and the repaired candidate.
verification: Each retry names both the prior diagnostic and the remedy it is testing.
The objective, protected expectation and cumulative budget remain intact across attempts.
The exit explains whether evidence is sufficient for review or which unresolved issue prevents further action.
outputs: Attempt ledger linking diagnostics, remedies, candidates and results.
Review-ready evidence or an explicit stop with the required next decision.
risks: An agent can overfit a visible failure while missing adjacent behavior.
Repeated rejection without useful diagnostics can consume resources and encourage unauthorized changes to the success criterion.

records.label: Maker–Checker: Separate Production from Acceptance
records.summary: Separate the responsibility for producing a candidate from the responsibility for checking its claims, while protecting the approved objective and expected results from both inappropriate edits and self-approval. Evaluate independence through the origin of expectations, available evidence and effective permissions. Two roles or two models can still share the same mistake and cannot replace accountable acceptance.
records.limitation: Role separation reduces one source of self-review but does not make errors independent; shared assumptions or editable oracles can undermine both roles.

attributes.label: Maker–Checker: Separate Production from Acceptance
attributes.required_revision: Compare with Adversarial Agent Pattern (PAT:080; historical alias SDD2:C5); separating roles does not automatically make their errors independent.
attributes.limitation: Role separation reduces one source of self-review but does not make errors independent; shared assumptions or editable oracles can undermine both roles.

practice.purpose: Give a candidate a meaningful opportunity to fail against evidence the maker did not define merely by observing its own output.
when_to_use: A wrong-but-green candidate would have a material consequence or be difficult for a reviewer to spot.
The workflow can separate candidate production, independent findings and final acceptance authority.
when_not_to_use: The checker simply repeats the maker's explanation or uses expectations generated from the candidate.
A second role adds ceremony while the maker can still rewrite the protected oracle.
prerequisites: Expected behavior derived from an authorized source with a protected revision.
Distinct effective permissions and result channels for maker, checker and acceptance owner.
steps: Define what the maker may change and exclude the approved contract and protected expected results from its write scope.
Give the checker the actual candidate, relevant authority and independently justified cases rather than only the maker's summary.
Have the checker seek discrepancies and report reproducible findings with locators, assumptions and uncertainty.
Return confirmed in-scope failures as bounded repair requests; send ambiguous requirements to their owner.
Present the renewed candidate and current evidence to the accountable reviewer, preserving the distinction between checked and accepted.
practice.example: Illustrative example: The maker changes how stored decisions replay. A checker runs an independently specified case requiring the original response to survive a policy update. It reports a concrete mismatch but cannot edit the candidate. The maker repairs the implementation without changing that expectation. The final reviewer inspects current results and decides whether the candidate can advance; no checker status alone grants release approval.
verification: The expected answer has an origin independent of the candidate's observed output.
Neither role can silently alter protected authority or convert its own claim into acceptance.
A known wrong candidate is rejected, and evidence is renewed after a relevant repair.
outputs: Role and permission map plus independently grounded findings.
Candidate-bound evidence and a separate acceptance disposition.
risks: Different model names can mask shared context gaps or the same faulty requirement.
A read-only checker cannot protect an expectation that the maker remains able to edit.

records.label: Skills and Context Engineering: Remove Intent Debt
records.summary: Package recurring work instructions as a maintained, versioned skill or context aid with an owner, applicability and source references. Separate procedural guidance from retrieved evidence, task state and tool permissions. The aim is to make missing or ambiguous intent visible and reduce repeated clarification where justified, without claiming that a larger instruction file removes all intent debt.
records.limitation: A reusable instruction can be stale, contradictory or inapplicable; more context does not guarantee better understanding and cannot grant authority or tool access.

attributes.label: Skills and Context Engineering: Remove Intent Debt
attributes.required_revision: Version skills with an owner and separate permissions; context cannot eliminate every form of intent debt.
attributes.limitation: A reusable instruction can be stale, contradictory or inapplicable; more context does not guarantee better understanding and cannot grant authority or tool access.

practice.purpose: Make recurring procedural knowledge reusable while preserving a clear path to the current authorized objective and its unresolved questions.
when_to_use: A repeated task has stable procedural steps that workers otherwise reconstruct inconsistently.
Recurring misunderstandings can be traced to omitted context or unclear precedence.
when_not_to_use: A one-off instruction would be generalized without evidence of reuse.
The proposed skill mixes tool credentials, authority decisions and unverified repository claims into one trusted block.
prerequisites: A named maintainer and a versioned source for the procedure.
Applicability conditions, required inputs, expected outputs and independently enforced permission boundaries.
steps: Identify the recurring failure and write only the procedural guidance needed to address it.
State scope, input requirements, evidence requirements and stop conditions, linking authoritative sources instead of copying mutable rules everywhere.
Version and review the guidance, separating stable instructions from task-specific state and retrieved material.
At use time, verify applicability and freshness against the current task and permissions; keep unresolved intent visible.
Record concrete failures or maintenance changes, then revise or retire the skill when it no longer provides useful guidance.
practice.example: Illustrative example: A team writes a release-note drafting skill that requires a defined revision range, source links and explicit exclusions. The skill explains the workflow but grants no publishing access and contains no permanent claim about which features are released. Each run obtains its current approved inputs. When the release process changes, the owner updates the version and records which old instructions should no longer be used.
verification: The skill identifies its owner, version, applicable tasks and renewal triggers.
A worker can distinguish procedural advice from evidence and authoritative decisions.
A useful trial checks the actual deliverable and exposes missing context rather than merely confirming the skill file was loaded.
outputs: Versioned, owned procedural guidance with source links.
Applicability and renewal record from actual uses.
risks: Accumulated instructions can conflict or crowd out the evidence needed for the present task.
An apparently official skill can launder an old assumption into a current requirement unless its authority and scope are checked.

records.label: Memory and Retrieval: Read What the Model Could Not Know
records.summary: Retrieve task-relevant information that is absent from the model's immediate context, preserving source, revision, validity and authority. Memory can contain past actions, semantic summaries, instructions or approved decisions, and those types are not interchangeable. A useful system can abstain when evidence is missing or conflicting instead of turning retrieved plausibility into approved knowledge.
records.limitation: Retrieval can return relevant but stale, incomplete or misleading material; ranking similarity does not establish truth, comprehension or permission to act.

attributes.label: Memory and Retrieval: Read What the Model Could Not Know
attributes.required_revision: Use retrieval with abstention, sources and validity; memory is not approved knowledge by definition.
attributes.limitation: Retrieval can return relevant but stale, incomplete or misleading material; ranking similarity does not establish truth, comprehension or permission to act.

practice.purpose: Ground a task in the information it actually needs while keeping uncertainty and conflicting sources available for review.
when_to_use: Repository-specific decisions, recent changes or task history are needed to answer the next question.
A long-running task needs selective access to evidence beyond a compact resume record.
when_not_to_use: The system treats the top-ranked passage as authoritative without checking its provenance.
A missing decision is being filled by a plausible historical analogy instead of being raised with its owner.
prerequisites: Source records with stable locators, revisions and validity scopes.
A distinction between instructions, evidence, task state and authoritative decisions.
steps: Define the information need and the type of claim required: observation, current rule, past event or procedural instruction.
Retrieve candidate sources and retain their identities, scope and dates or versions relevant to the task.
Check applicability and authority, consulting original records when a derived summary cannot resolve a consequential claim.
Present supported facts separately from inferences, conflicts and omissions; abstain on unresolved questions that affect acceptance.
Bind useful retrieved evidence to the task record and set renewal triggers for any derived memory reused later.
practice.example: Illustrative example: A resumed agent finds two cards describing different policy thresholds. It checks the source revisions and discovers that one governs historical decisions while the other governs new requests. It retrieves the approved delta and preserves both scoped facts. If the relevant approval record is unavailable, it reports that gap instead of choosing the newer-looking card as authority.
verification: Material claims can be traced from a summary back to the source used.
Current applicability and authority are checked independently of retrieval rank or recency.
Missing or contradictory evidence produces an explicit uncertainty or owner question rather than a fabricated answer.
outputs: Task-specific evidence set with provenance and applicability.
Derived memory or answer that distinguishes supported claims, inference and unresolved gaps.
risks: Retrieved instructions embedded in untrusted material can attempt to cross the tool-permission boundary.
A compressed memory card may omit the qualifier that determines whether a fact applies to the present task.

records.label: Connectors and Tools: Move Exact Work Outside the Weights
records.summary: Delegate exact retrieval, computation or controlled operations to tools whose interfaces and outputs can be checked. The model selects or explains work while the executor performs the specified operation within an enforced permission envelope. Deterministic arithmetic or successful API execution establishes only that operation's result; it does not authorize the external effect or validate the task's underlying assumptions.
records.limitation: An exact executor can faithfully perform the wrong request against stale data; tool success is not proof of business correctness, appropriate access or authorized effects.

attributes.label: Connectors and Tools: Move Exact Work Outside the Weights
attributes.required_revision: Use exact executors with explicit interfaces and permissions; exact calculation does not authorize external effects.
attributes.limitation: An exact executor can faithfully perform the wrong request against stale data; tool success is not proof of business correctness, appropriate access or authorized effects.

practice.purpose: Move operations requiring precise execution into inspectable tools while keeping interpretation and authority decisions explicit.
when_to_use: A task needs reproducible calculations, repository queries or structured transformations.
A supported connector can perform a clearly authorized operation more reliably than manual transcription.
when_not_to_use: The requested operation or destination exceeds the task's authority.
The interface cannot identify what data or external resource the operation will affect.
prerequisites: A documented input and output contract with the relevant data or resource identity.
An external enforcement point for access, effect scope and applicable budgets.
steps: Define the operation precisely, including units, source version, target resource and any side effects.
Check input assumptions and authorization before dispatch; use a read-only or preview operation when that answers the task.
Execute through the controlled interface and capture the actual status, output and relevant provenance.
Validate the result against the expected shape and meaning, distinguishing executor errors from incorrect assumptions in the request.
Use the result only for its supported purpose and require any separate authority needed for a consequential follow-on action.
practice.example: Illustrative example: An agent calculates the changed and added files between two website packages using a script over file hashes. The script can determine exact byte differences for those inputs. The agent still checks that the chosen baseline is the published package. Producing a correct delta does not grant permission to upload it to the public site or to alter unrelated repository settings.
verification: Inputs identify the intended source, target, units and revision unambiguously.
The recorded tool result concerns the operation actually requested, with failures preserved.
A precise output is not used to infer an approval or effect outside the operation's authority.
outputs: Structured operation record with inputs, output and source identity.
Validated result and any separate decision required for its use.
risks: A broadly scoped connector can turn a small interpretation error into a consequential external write.
Silent coercion, stale resource selection or missing units can produce a precise but misleading result.

records.label: Worktrees: Isolate the Write Domains
records.summary: Use separate worktrees or equivalent isolated checkouts so concurrent workers produce changes in distinct write domains. Tie each workspace to an input revision and a named task, then integrate deliberately with fresh evidence. Filesystem separation prevents some edit collisions, but ownership of the logical outcome and shared external resources still require explicit coordination.
records.limitation: Worktrees isolate working files, not necessarily credentials, services or task meaning; two isolated workers can still duplicate or contradict the same logical change.

attributes.label: Worktrees: Isolate the Write Domains
attributes.required_revision: Isolate writes, while recognizing that this does not prevent logical duplication of tasks.
attributes.limitation: Worktrees isolate working files, not necessarily credentials, services or task meaning; two isolated workers can still duplicate or contradict the same logical change.

practice.purpose: Keep concurrent candidate changes inspectable and recoverable until a designated integration point reconciles them.
when_to_use: Independent implementation tasks can proceed without sharing mutable working files.
Alternative candidates need to be compared against the same baseline before selecting one.
when_not_to_use: Workers require concurrent uncoordinated access to one shared database or authoritative artifact.
Creating separate directories is being treated as sufficient protection against overlapping logical responsibilities.
prerequisites: A baseline revision and an ownership map for logical targets.
A named integrator and controls for shared resources outside the working directories.
steps: Assign a unique task and target to each workspace, recording the baseline and permitted write scope.
Create or select the isolated checkout and verify its state before work begins, preserving any existing user work.
Keep candidate artifacts and checks associated with their workspace and revision rather than a shared mutable status file.
Review dependencies and integrate selected changes through the owner, resolving semantic conflicts as well as textual conflicts.
Renew relevant checks on the integrated candidate and retire workspaces only after required artifacts and unresolved work are accounted for.
practice.example: Illustrative example: One worker updates export documentation while another repairs an independent parser test in a separate checkout. The coordinator discovers that both also propose renaming the same public option. That logical overlap is resolved by assigning one owner, even though the files were edited in isolation. After integration, the combined documentation and behavior checks run against the resulting revision.
verification: Each workspace has the expected baseline, owner and allowed target.
The coordinator detects duplicate logical changes and shared-resource dependencies before integration.
The accepted evidence belongs to the integrated candidate, including any resolution of conflicts.
outputs: Workspace-to-task map with isolated candidate artifacts.
Integration record, renewed checks and accounted-for remaining work.
risks: Shared credentials or service endpoints can bypass the intended separation of write effects.
Conflict-free textual merges can still combine incompatible assumptions about behavior or interfaces.

records.label: Multi-Loop Coordination: One Owner per Target
records.summary: Assign one current owner to each logical target across concurrent loops, using bounded work concessions or leases where needed. Ownership names the task, contract revision, validity and generation so stale workers cannot submit as current. Coordination must operate above filenames and preserve decision rights, because separate files can encode the same policy or competing implementations.
records.limitation: A sequential ownership check is not a proof of distributed locking; real concurrency, failures and identity controls require an implementation suited to the environment.

attributes.label: Multi-Loop Coordination: One Owner per Target
attributes.required_revision: Own the target above file level and manage leases explicitly.
attributes.limitation: A sequential ownership check is not a proof of distributed locking; real concurrency, failures and identity controls require an implementation suited to the environment.

practice.purpose: Prevent duplicate or stale work from entering integration under an apparently valid assignment.
when_to_use: Several agents or repeated triggers can act on the same backlog item or logical component.
A task can outlive its original contract revision, assignment or coordinator session.
when_not_to_use: No shared mutable or duplicate target exists and a lease system would add needless complexity.
A local example is assumed to provide race-safe distributed ownership without further implementation.
prerequisites: Canonical target identities and a coordinator able to grant, renew and revoke assignments.
A state record containing owner, task, contract revision, expiry and assignment generation.
steps: Define logical targets so semantically overlapping changes cannot evade ownership by touching different files.
Grant a bounded assignment only when the target is available and its prerequisites and review capacity are satisfied.
Require progress and submissions to carry the current assignment identity, intention revision and candidate evidence.
On expiry, cancellation or changed intention, invalidate affected concessions and preserve prior work as historical or pending reconciliation.
Accept a submission for review only after checking its current assignment and evidence, then release or explicitly transfer ownership.
practice.example: Illustrative example: A worker receives the task of updating a pricing rule, while another investigates its documentation. The policy revision changes before the first worker submits. Its old assignment and green tests are retained but rejected as current evidence. The coordinator grants a new generation after the owner resolves the change, preventing the delayed old submission from overwriting the newly assigned work.
verification: Competing requests for the same logical target cannot both obtain current ownership under the implemented model.
Stale generations, expired leases and duplicate event identities have explicit outcomes.
Submission checks use current authority and evidence, not only the state recorded when work started.
outputs: Target ownership and concession history with explicit invalidations.
Current submissions, rejected stale events and unresolved integration decisions.
risks: Clock assumptions, race conditions or coordinator failures can undermine a naive lease implementation.
A poorly defined target map can allow two owners to change the same business rule through different artifacts.

records.label: Budget and Observability: Price the Next Attempt
records.summary: Before another attempt, estimate its incremental burden and compare that decision with the cumulative task record. Include setup, generation, tools, verification, review, waiting and rejected work without double-counting. Use observations where available and label uncertain inputs. A cheap next call may still be a poor choice when checking capacity, authority or the probability of useful progress is missing.
records.limitation: Cost estimates depend on task mix and uncertain outcomes; benchmark performance or token prices alone cannot establish the return of this local workflow.

attributes.label: Budget and Observability: Price the Next Attempt
attributes.required_revision: Track next-step and total cost, including setup and rejected attempts; do not transfer returns from benchmarks.
attributes.limitation: Cost estimates depend on task mix and uncertain outcomes; benchmark performance or token prices alone cannot establish the return of this local workflow.

practice.purpose: Make continuation an explicit engineering and economic decision while preserving required controls as eligibility conditions.
when_to_use: A loop can spend more time or resources on repeated attempts, extra agents or another review stage.
A team compares candidate execution routes for the same class of accepted changes.
when_not_to_use: The proposed saving comes from omitting a required permission or independent check.
Only inference cost is available but the result is presented as total delivery cost.
prerequisites: A task ledger with stable event identities and distinct cost or time categories.
An eligible next action and explicit assumptions for unobserved costs or outcomes.
steps: Record costs already incurred, including failed attempts and initial setup, with observed and estimated values distinguishable.
Identify the next permitted action and the diagnostic or uncertainty it is expected to resolve.
Estimate its marginal execution, checking, reviewer and integration burden, accounting for existing capacity constraints.
Compare continuing, simplifying, using a human-led route or stopping under the same required controls.
Authorize the eligible choice through the task's existing budget rules, then record the actual outcome to improve later estimates.
practice.example: Illustrative example: After two unsuccessful repairs, a team considers a third model run or a short maintainer investigation. The ledger includes setup, tool use and the review already spent, while the next-step estimate separates those sunk costs from the new decision. An unresolved policy question makes another generation attempt ineligible regardless of its small token cost; the team routes the question to its owner.
verification: Cumulative accounting includes abandoned and rejected work as well as accepted results.
Person-time, elapsed waiting and cash charges are reported distinctly before aggregation.
The chosen action has both a valid permission path and a plausible information benefit under stated assumptions.
outputs: Task cost ledger and next-action decision with assumptions.
Observed outcome, remaining budget and any revised continuation threshold.
risks: Ignoring review and integration can make a low-cost producer appear efficient while total accepted-change cost rises.
A precise spreadsheet can hide uncertainty about acceptance, correlated retries or rare consequential failures.

records.label: Safety and Guardrails: Verification Is Not Authorization
records.summary: Keep three questions separate: whether an operation is permitted, whether its result satisfies a check, and who may accept or publish the change. Enforce the permission envelope before execution and evaluate evidence afterward. A passing test, clean scanner or policy-shaped file supplies only its specific finding; none silently grants the authority of a neighboring decision.
records.limitation: Verification can establish selected predicates without authenticating an approver or covering unmodeled effects; authorization cannot manufacture evidence that was never obtained.

attributes.label: Safety and Guardrails: Verification Is Not Authorization
attributes.required_revision: Verification, policy and authorization remain distinct decisions.
attributes.limitation: Verification can establish selected predicates without authenticating an approver or covering unmodeled effects; authorization cannot manufacture evidence that was never obtained.
attributes.family_name: Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

practice.purpose: Prevent technical success from being used to cross a boundary that requires a different owner's authority.
when_to_use: A workflow passes from candidate creation through review toward a consequential external action.
Several checks and actors contribute evidence that could be mistaken for one combined approval.
when_not_to_use: An established workflow already separates permissions, checks and acceptance; map the practice to those controls instead of introducing parallel approval stages.
A small, pre-authorized edit has a clear owner and verification path; retain that path without adding redundant decision stages.
prerequisites: Named decision rights for scope, tool access, acceptance and any external publication or release.
Checks whose supported claims and unverified boundaries are explicit.
steps: Map the next operation to the actor, target and existing authority that would permit it.
Enforce that permission before the tool acts, independently of the model's confidence or expected result.
Run the relevant checks and record their actual scope, candidate revision and limitations.
Present the evidence to the role responsible for the next decision, preserving any missing authority or unresolved risk.
Record that decision separately and recheck applicability if the candidate, contract, destination or permissions change.
practice.example: Illustrative example: An agent creates a patch that passes functional tests and a dependency scan. Those findings support review of the candidate, but the task only authorizes local preparation. The release owner still decides deployment through the established process. Conversely, an owner may authorize a release review, but that permission cannot be described as evidence that an unrun security check passed.
verification: No successful test or scanner result changes the execution permission profile.
The acceptance or publication decision identifies the responsible authority and the exact eligible candidate.
Missing evidence and missing authorization remain distinguishable in the final status.
outputs: Decision-rights map and enforced operation outcomes.
Candidate evidence plus a separate, scoped decision record.
risks: Combining all statuses into one green indicator can conceal which obligation remains unmet.
Repository text or generated metadata can impersonate an approval unless the real identity and authority path are checked.

records.label: Daily Triage: rank the rare urgent item
records.summary: Use a bounded triage pass to identify a small set of potentially urgent items from a larger stream, showing the evidence and uncertainty behind their proposed order. Preserve deferred work and route consequential cases to the right owner. This optional companion workflow proposes priorities; ranking an issue does not authorize a fix, a policy change or a message to an external party.
records.limitation: A triage model can miss a rare urgent case or over-rank persuasive text; usefulness depends on the queue, evidence quality and the owner's review capacity.

attributes.label: Daily Triage: rank the rare urgent item
attributes.required_revision: An optional triage example; proposed priority is not an authorized change.
attributes.limitation: A triage model can miss a rare urgent case or over-rank persuasive text; usefulness depends on the queue, evidence quality and the owner's review capacity.

practice.purpose: Focus limited human attention on items whose delay may matter, without converting automated ranking into unattended execution.
when_to_use: A queue is large enough that manually scanning every item repeatedly imposes a real burden.
The team can state what makes an item urgent and who decides its disposition.
when_not_to_use: The ranking would automatically trigger consequential actions without the queue owner's decision.
Available item descriptions omit the evidence needed to distinguish urgency from confident wording.
prerequisites: A bounded source queue and explicit priority or escalation criteria.
A named triage owner with capacity to examine the proposed urgent set and a record of deferred items.
steps: Capture the queue snapshot and the time window, preserving item identity and current status.
Apply the stated criteria using linked evidence, separating urgency, impact, uncertainty and age where they mean different things.
Produce a small ranked proposal with reasons, missing information and any rule-based mandatory escalation.
Have the owner review uncertain or consequential cases and record a disposition without silently dropping the rest.
Review outcomes later, including missed urgent items and false alarms, and adjust the triage criteria or assistance only from those observations.
practice.example: Illustrative example: A daily repository queue contains many documentation suggestions and one report of changed replay behavior. The assistant flags the replay report because its linked reproduction may violate a protected invariant, while labeling the evidence incomplete. The owner checks the report and assigns the next action. The assistant's ranking does not permit it to change the replay policy or contact affected customers.
verification: Each proposed urgent item has a traceable reason tied to the stated criteria.
Deferred and unassessed items remain visible, including relevant ageing or follow-up needs.
Evaluation counts false alarms and missed urgent cases rather than only correct top-ranked suggestions.
outputs: Ranked triage proposal with evidence, uncertainties and retained backlog.
Owner dispositions and later outcome observations.
risks: Overfitting the criteria to common items can hide the rare event the process was meant to surface.
Automated urgency labels can consume scarce review capacity and displace quieter but consequential work.

records.label: CI Sweeper: classify before fixing
records.summary: Inspect failed continuous-integration work and classify the evidence before deciding whether a code repair is warranted. Distinguish a candidate regression, known baseline failure, environmental problem, potentially intermittent behavior and unresolved cause. The optional sweeper creates a routed diagnostic or bounded repair proposal; it does not infer that every red build is a software defect the agent may fix.
records.limitation: A classifier or a later passing rerun cannot reliably establish the cause of intermittent failures; evidence may remain insufficient to distinguish code, test and environment.

attributes.label: CI Sweeper: classify before fixing
attributes.required_revision: Classify a red build before repairing it; do not guarantee that a classifier can recognize flakiness.
attributes.limitation: A classifier or a later passing rerun cannot reliably establish the cause of intermittent failures; evidence may remain insufficient to distinguish code, test and environment.

practice.purpose: Reduce indiscriminate CI repair by making the failure type, candidate identity and appropriate owner explicit first.
when_to_use: Many failed jobs require initial diagnosis before maintainers can assign work.
The same repository has both candidate regressions and infrastructure or pre-existing failures.
when_not_to_use: The workflow reruns jobs until green and discards the failed observations.
The proposed repair crosses the current task scope or weakens a required check.
prerequisites: Job logs, exact candidate and baseline identities, and relevant environment information.
An agreed classification vocabulary that permits unknown and an owner for each route.
steps: Capture the failure signature, command, revision, timing and environment details before logs expire or another run replaces them.
Compare the failure with the baseline and available related runs, avoiding claims unsupported by missing history.
Classify the evidence with a confidence boundary and list the observation needed to resolve competing explanations.
For a reproducible in-scope regression, create a bounded repair request; otherwise route the diagnostic to the appropriate maintainer or infrastructure owner.
Retain reruns and final dispositions so later success does not erase the original failure or create a false causal explanation.
practice.example: Illustrative example: A build fails during package retrieval before any changed code runs. A later rerun succeeds. The sweeper records an environmental candidate explanation and the two run identities, but does not declare the test flaky or alter source code. Another failure reproduces on the patch and not the baseline, providing a stronger basis for a focused repair proposal to the component owner.
verification: A classification is supported by actual runs and clearly separates observations from inferred causes.
A passing rerun does not delete the failure or automatically satisfy policies requiring investigation.
Any proposed repair has a relevant owner, bounded scope and evidence that distinguishes it from unrelated work.
outputs: Failure classification with diagnostic evidence and unresolved hypotheses.
Routed owner decision or scoped repair proposal with retained run history.
risks: Grouping failures by similar log text can combine unrelated causes.
Repeated reruns can hide an unstable environment and consume capacity without yielding a useful diagnosis.

records.label: Dependency Sweeper: route by risk
records.summary: Route dependency updates according to their specific compatibility, provenance and effect risks instead of treating all version changes alike. Establish the package identity and proposed change, inspect relevant evidence, and create a proportionate review path. This optional maintenance workflow produces a candidate and risk record; passing CI does not authorize a dependency's adoption, its permissions or the merge.
records.limitation: Version labels, release notes and passing tests can miss consequential compatibility or supply-chain changes; risk cannot be inferred from a version increment alone.

attributes.label: Dependency Sweeper: route by risk
attributes.required_revision: Route updates by risk; green CI does not authorize the dependency or the merge.
attributes.limitation: Version labels, release notes and passing tests can miss consequential compatibility or supply-chain changes; risk cannot be inferred from a version increment alone.
attributes.family_name: Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

practice.purpose: Make dependency maintenance reviewable by connecting each proposed update to the behavior, trust boundary and owner it affects.
when_to_use: A repository has recurring dependency updates that require different levels of investigation.
A maintainer needs to separate routine candidates from updates changing interfaces, build behavior or execution privileges.
when_not_to_use: Package identity or provenance is uncertain and the proposed automation would install first and investigate later.
The route assumes every patch-level version is harmless or every passing update may merge unattended.
prerequisites: A known dependency baseline, lock or resolution record, and authorized update scope.
A dependency owner and access to relevant upstream or repository evidence.
steps: Identify the exact package, source, resolved version and proposed version, including transitive changes that affect the candidate.
Review relevant compatibility notes, provenance and build or runtime effects, retaining unknowns rather than inventing reassurance.
Route the candidate by the actual affected boundaries and project rules, assigning specialist review when justified.
Prepare the bounded update and run checks relevant to its use, including behavior that may not be covered by installation success.
Present the changed resolution, evidence and residual uncertainty for the authorized adoption and integration decision.
practice.example: Illustrative example: A dependency update changes only a declared version in the manifest but also changes the resolved parser used by the application. The sweeper records that transitive difference and proposes compatibility cases for the input formats the service supports. Even if those cases pass, the maintainer still assesses package provenance and the project-specific approval path before accepting the update.
verification: The candidate's actual resolution matches the package identities and versions in the review record.
Checks cover the dependency's consequential local use rather than merely a successful install.
Unknown provenance, new privileges or compatibility gaps remain visible to the responsible approver.
outputs: Dependency change inventory and evidence-based routing decision.
Bounded update candidate with checks, owner and residual risks.
risks: A harmless-looking top-level update can alter transitive code or installation behavior.
Treating vulnerability scanning as a complete safety verdict can miss provenance, licensing or operational questions outside its scope.

records.label: Duplicate detection
records.summary: Use retrieval or similarity analysis to propose records that may describe the same underlying issue, practice or change, then confirm the semantic relationship before consolidation. Preserve stable identifiers, source evidence and historical dispositions. A duplicate candidate may instead be a related topic, a recurrence, a different affected version or a distinct request with similar wording.
records.limitation: Similarity scores cannot establish semantic identity; deduplication can lose meaningful history or merge incompatible obligations if performed without contextual review.

attributes.label: Duplicate detection
attributes.required_revision: Confirm retrieval-proposed duplicates semantically and preserve historical records.
attributes.limitation: Similarity scores cannot establish semantic identity; deduplication can lose meaningful history or merge incompatible obligations if performed without contextual review.

practice.purpose: Reduce repeated investigation while retaining distinctions needed for ownership, version history and accountable decisions.
when_to_use: A catalogue or issue queue contains repeated titles, paraphrases or overlapping reports.
Maintainers need to locate prior work before deciding whether a new item is genuinely redundant.
when_not_to_use: The source records lack enough evidence to determine whether they concern the same behavior.
The process would delete or close items automatically based only on textual similarity.
prerequisites: Stable record identifiers with source links, affected versions and current status.
A responsible reviewer and a way to represent related, duplicate, recurring and unresolved relationships.
steps: Retrieve candidate pairs or groups using labels, content and relevant metadata, retaining the basis for the suggestion.
Compare the underlying outcome, affected component, version, reproduction and requested action rather than the title alone.
Classify the relationship explicitly and identify any uncertainty that needs the record owner.
If consolidation is justified, choose a canonical navigation target while preserving every original record and its provenance.
Link the records and retain their historical dispositions, ensuring searches can still discover aliases and explain the consolidation.
practice.example: Illustrative example: Two issue titles both say export order is unstable. One concerns the current CSV endpoint; the other concerns historical PDF reports and has a different reproduction. The system proposes them as similar, but the maintainer marks them related rather than duplicate. Two genuinely identical reports can point to one investigation while their original reporters' evidence and affected revisions remain intact.
verification: Each duplicate decision states the shared underlying behavior and the evidence supporting identity.
Canonical navigation preserves original identifiers, provenance and any version-specific exceptions.
A review sample checks false merges and missed duplicates, including records with misleadingly similar titles.
outputs: Candidate duplicate report and reviewed relationship decisions.
Canonical links or aliases with preserved original history.
risks: Collapsing separate incidents can hide repeated failures that should inform maintenance priorities.
Retaining only the most complete-looking record can discard a counterexample that changes the diagnosis.

records.label: PR babysitter
records.summary: Monitor a pull request's current candidate, required checks, review findings and unresolved dependencies to propose its next action. Bind every readiness claim to the exact revision and relevant authority. This optional companion workflow helps maintainers follow evidence as a PR changes; it must distinguish a truly eligible review candidate from a false-ready status based on stale or incomplete information.
records.limitation: PR status can lag behind changing code, base branches or policy; a green dashboard and absence of comments do not prove review readiness or acceptance.

attributes.label: PR babysitter
attributes.required_revision: Base PR status on evidence for the correct revision; record false-ready as a distinct outcome.
attributes.limitation: PR status can lag behind changing code, base branches or policy; a green dashboard and absence of comments do not prove review readiness or acceptance.

practice.purpose: Reduce forgotten review obligations without replacing the maintainer's decision with an automated status summary.
when_to_use: Pull requests wait across multiple revisions, checks and reviewer exchanges.
Maintainers need a compact view of what specifically blocks the next legitimate stage.
when_not_to_use: The monitor would merge because checks appear green or comments have been answered.
It cannot determine whether a result or review applies to the current candidate.
prerequisites: Access to current candidate and base identities, required checks and review dispositions.
A project-defined readiness policy and a named owner for exceptions or acceptance.
steps: Capture the current PR revision, relevant base, contract or requirement revision and mandatory evidence.
Associate each check and substantive review finding with the candidate it actually concerns.
Identify stale evidence, unresolved findings, missing decisions and dependency changes rather than flattening them into one status.
Propose the next bounded action, such as rerunning a check, requesting a clarification or presenting a current bundle to the reviewer.
Recompute readiness after changes and retain false-ready incidents as an explicit outcome for improving the monitor.
practice.example: Illustrative example: A pull request passed checks, then received a new commit adjusting replay behavior. The monitor finds that the visible approval and independent replay result concern the previous revision. It reports the precise stale evidence and prepares the current diff for review. Answering the earlier comment or seeing one green job does not restore readiness until the applicable evidence is renewed under the repository's policy.
verification: Every required result and review disposition matches the revision or supported scope claimed.
A newly pushed commit or relevant base change invalidates only the evidence whose applicability must be renewed.
The monitor can demonstrate a false-ready case and reports it separately from ordinary waiting.
outputs: Revision-specific readiness report with blockers and next actions.
Evidence renewal and disposition history, including false-ready observations.
risks: Automated reminders can add noise or pressure without resolving the actual missing decision.
A stale approval can look authoritative when its associated candidate identity is hidden.

records.label: Post-merge cleanup
records.summary: Inspect the integrated result for justified follow-up maintenance, such as obsolete temporary artifacts, duplicated explanations or incomplete handoff notes. Produce scoped proposals with evidence and ownership before making further changes. Merge is a new baseline for inspection, not standing permission for broad cleanup or proof that every leftover item is safe to remove.
records.limitation: Apparently unused code, files or branches may still support consumers, rollback or historical explanation; cleanup evidence can be incomplete.

attributes.label: Post-merge cleanup
attributes.required_revision: Use this as a source of maintenance proposals, not automatic authorization to rewrite.
attributes.limitation: Apparently unused code, files or branches may still support consumers, rollback or historical explanation; cleanup evidence can be incomplete.

practice.purpose: Keep integration from leaving avoidable maintenance burden while preserving the obligations and history needed by the next engineer.
when_to_use: A completed change leaves known temporary scaffolding or an explicitly deferred maintenance item.
Integration reveals duplicated or outdated material that a maintainer should assess.
when_not_to_use: The proposed cleanup has no demonstrated consequence beyond aesthetic preference.
Deletion could remove user work, recovery evidence or a consumer whose existence has not been checked.
prerequisites: An identified integrated baseline and the original task's actual cleanup authorization.
An owner for each affected target and evidence of the artifact's current purpose or obsolescence.
steps: Inspect the integrated diff and deferred-work record for specific follow-up candidates rather than scanning for unrestricted rewrites.
For each candidate, identify its purpose, consumers, retention needs and the consequence of leaving or changing it.
Separate cleanup already authorized by the task from new maintenance proposals that need their own scope decision.
Apply eligible changes in a bounded candidate and verify the relevant behavior, documentation or recovery path.
Record the outcome and preserve the rationale for retained items or deferred proposals so a later sweeper does not rediscover the same uncertainty.
practice.example: Illustrative example: After an API migration merges, a temporary compatibility note appears outdated. The maintainer checks that the old endpoint still serves one documented client, so the note remains with a revised validity statement. An unused migration scratch file can be removed within the authorized cleanup scope. A broader rewrite of the adapter becomes a separate proposal with its own behavior and review requirements.
verification: Each removal or rewrite has evidence about its purpose and affected consumers.
The candidate stays within explicit cleanup authority and preserves required historical or recovery artifacts.
Relevant checks run on the integrated baseline rather than an obsolete pre-merge workspace.
outputs: Scoped maintenance proposal or authorized cleanup candidate.
Verified result and rationale for items retained, changed or deferred.
risks: Broad cleanup can obscure the original change and create unrelated regressions.
Deleting evidence too early can make later diagnosis or rollback reasoning harder even when the running code is unaffected.

records.label: Changelog drafter
records.summary: Draft a changelog from a defined change range and attributable evidence, separating implemented changes, user-visible effects, unresolved work and actual release status. Preserve links that let a reviewer challenge each material statement. The draft communicates verified scope; it is not itself proof that work completed, was accepted, reached production or produced the claimed benefit.
records.limitation: Commits and PR descriptions can misstate behavior or deployment status; a coherent narrative can still omit breaking effects or promote unfinished work.

attributes.label: Changelog drafter
attributes.required_revision: Provide a sourced draft for review; release notes are not evidence of completion.
attributes.limitation: Commits and PR descriptions can misstate behavior or deployment status; a coherent narrative can still omit breaking effects or promote unfinished work.

practice.purpose: Turn a set of changes into an accurate reader-facing account without letting generated prose enlarge the delivered scope.
when_to_use: A release or update has a clear baseline and target whose differences need explanation.
Maintainers need a concise draft that traces claims to the accepted change record.
when_not_to_use: The release range or actual publication status is unknown.
The draft would infer user benefits or completed work from plans, commit messages or unreviewed proposals alone.
prerequisites: Identified baseline and target revisions with relevant issue, diff and verification records.
An editor or release owner who can confirm the audience, terminology and publication status.
steps: Establish the exact comparison range and distinguish accepted changes from proposals, reverted work and unrelated commits.
Inspect the actual diff and supporting records, identifying externally meaningful behavior and any compatibility or migration implications.
Draft concise claims linked to their evidence, labeling unknown deployment or validation status rather than filling gaps.
Have the responsible reviewer check completeness, wording, breaking effects and the relationship between code changes and actual release.
Publish only through the authorized process and preserve the reviewed range and evidence links for future correction.
practice.example: Illustrative example: A website update translates practice descriptions and adds a catalogue collection. The draft points to the changed catalogue data and verified navigation, while distinguishing those completed package changes from deployment to the public site. It does not say the update is live merely because a ZIP exists. A reviewer checks the range and removes a claim about unrelated articles that were not changed in this release.
verification: Every material statement is supported by the selected change range and relevant evidence.
The text distinguishes implementation, acceptance, publication and measured outcomes where those statuses differ.
Known incompatibilities, required user actions and incomplete work are accurately represented.
outputs: Reviewed changelog draft with evidence links and defined revision range.
Publication disposition and any unresolved wording or status questions.
risks: An attractive summary can overstate the scope by repeating a PR's original ambition.
Grouping changes too aggressively can hide an action users must take or an important compatibility boundary.

records.label: Capstone orchestra
records.summary: Compose several practices around one concrete capstone task only when each mechanism addresses a named uncertainty and justifies its marginal cost. Define the authorized outcome, shared evidence and decision rights before coordinating components. This retained companion concept is an integration exercise, not evidence that a large orchestration stack improves every task or that course materials establish operational results.
records.limitation: An impressive multi-component demonstration can conceal duplicated work and correlated errors; exercise completion does not establish production value or independently retained skill.

attributes.label: Capstone orchestra
attributes.required_revision: Composition is useful only when it justifies marginal cost; verify course data before reusing it.
attributes.limitation: An impressive multi-component demonstration can conceal duplicated work and correlated errors; exercise completion does not establish production value or independently retained skill.

practice.purpose: Assess whether the selected mechanisms work together to deliver one accountable outcome at an acceptable total burden.
when_to_use: A learning or pilot task needs to examine interactions among scope, execution, verification, review and handoff.
Simpler routes have an identified limitation that an added mechanism could plausibly address.
when_not_to_use: The objective is to demonstrate as many agents or tools as possible.
Course examples, completion statistics or cost inputs have not been checked but would be presented as observed results.
prerequisites: A bounded task contract, independent outcome checks and a named integration owner.
A simpler eligible comparison route plus a ledger for setup, coordination, verification and review.
steps: State the outcome and consequential uncertainties, including the minimum controls required regardless of the chosen machinery.
Assign a purpose to every proposed component and omit those that do not change a necessary decision or useful observation.
Define interfaces, ownership, permission boundaries and evidence identities so one component cannot assume another's authority.
Run the bounded composition, retaining failures, handoff losses, rejected work and the actual integration burden.
Evaluate the accepted result and the marginal value of each mechanism, then simplify or stop where the evidence does not support keeping it.
practice.example: Illustrative example: A capstone updates a small service and its documentation. The team compares an interactive route with a bounded maker and an independent checker, using the same requirements and behavior cases. It records setup, review and integration effort rather than counting generated artifacts. An additional debate agent is omitted because no unresolved decision needs it; any educational benefit is assessed separately through the learner's later independent work.
verification: Every retained component has a named purpose, output and accountable integration boundary.
The outcome evidence concerns the integrated candidate and preserves required independence and authority.
Cost or learning conclusions distinguish observed pilot results, assumptions, unverified course claims and unknown follow-up.
outputs: Composition and decision record with integrated candidate evidence.
Cost and learning observations, plus reasons to keep, simplify or retire mechanisms.
risks: A complex demonstration can reward visible activity while shifting the real burden into review.
Reusing illustrative course inputs as measurements can create a fabricated return or effectiveness claim.
practice.editorial_note: Editorial operational guidance expanded for Atlas v13.1 from the retained practice descriptor, NDSE2 Chapter 13's practice-selection guidance and Chapter 12's thematic guidance. The historical family is F12. The example is illustrative, not a reported study.

records.label: Spec-First Generation
records.summary: Establish the intended behavior and representative scenarios before asking an assistant to generate a candidate implementation. The specification states obligations that an accountable owner has authorized; the implementation plan proposes how to satisfy them. Keep these separate so a convenient design cannot quietly redefine success.
records.limitation: A specification can be internally clear yet omit a consequential stakeholder requirement; generation does not resolve that omission.

attributes.label: Spec-First Generation
attributes.required_revision: Establish authorized intention and scenarios before the candidate; keep the specification distinct from the plan.
attributes.limitation: A specification can be internally clear yet omit a consequential stakeholder requirement; generation does not resolve that omission.

practice.purpose: Make the acceptance question inspectable before implementation choices begin to shape the apparent requirements.
when_to_use: A change affects observable behavior, compatibility, policy, or an interface used by others.
Several implementations are plausible and reviewers need a common basis for judging them.
when_not_to_use: The purpose is still an exploratory hypothesis; first authorize a bounded experiment and label its provisional assumptions.
prerequisites: A named owner can resolve consequential behavior questions.
Existing obligations, affected consumers, and authoritative scenarios are accessible.
steps: Describe outcomes, boundaries, exclusions, and failure behavior without prescribing unnecessary implementation details.
Write ordinary, boundary, and negative scenarios; record where each expected result comes from.
Resolve blocking questions with the owner and version the approved answers together with remaining explicit unknowns.
Ask for an implementation plan that references the obligations; reject plan choices that silently change them.
Generate within the permitted scope, then compare the candidate with the approved scenarios and required regressions.
practice.example: Illustrative example: A service must preserve the response originally stored for a repeated request. The specification records the request identity, permitted payload, and expected historical response before an agent chooses a storage design. When the agent proposes reevaluating the request under current policy, the owner can identify a contract violation without debating the programming language or persistence library.
verification: Each material acceptance claim traces to an authorized behavior statement.
The plan can change without changing the approved expected outcomes.
Unresolved high-consequence questions block the affected candidate rather than becoming implementation assumptions.
outputs: A versioned behavior contract with scenarios.
A separately revisable implementation plan and an impact list.
risks: Copying implementation behavior into the specification can preserve an existing defect.
An elaborate document may hide a missing decision behind polished prose.
practice.editorial_note: Editorial operational guidance expanded for Atlas v13.1 from the retained practice descriptor and NDSE2 Chapters 4 and 13 thematic guidance. Family F04 preserves the catalogue classification. The example is illustrative; this entry does not establish measured effectiveness.

records.label: Test-Driven AI Development
records.summary: Write and examine tests before AI-assisted implementation, deriving expected results from an independently authorized behavior reference. Preserve the initial failing case, implement a bounded change, and rerun the relevant checks. The value comes from the quality and protection of the oracle, not merely the order in which files were created.
records.limitation: Passing tests establish behavior for their checked conditions; even independent expectations do not provide complete defect coverage.

attributes.label: Test-Driven AI Development
attributes.required_revision: Test-first work requires independently grounded expected results; a green result is local to its oracle.
attributes.limitation: Passing tests establish behavior for their checked conditions; even independent expectations do not provide complete defect coverage.

practice.purpose: Prevent a candidate and its generated tests from agreeing on the same incorrect interpretation of required behavior.
when_to_use: A defect has a reproducible input and an authoritative expected outcome.
New behavior can be expressed through examples, invariants, or an established interface contract.
when_not_to_use: Expected behavior is disputed or unavailable; clarify it before treating an assertion as an acceptance oracle.
prerequisites: A protected expectation source and a reproducible test environment.
The maker cannot silently rewrite mandatory acceptance checks.
steps: Identify the requirement and independently derive the expected result, retaining its version and owner.
Create a focused check and confirm that it fails on the relevant wrong behavior for the intended reason.
Record the failure before implementation; distinguish a meaningful assertion failure from broken test setup.
Let the maker implement the smallest coherent repair while retaining the approved expectation.
Rerun the focused check and mandatory regressions; keep maker-written supplementary tests clearly identified.
practice.example: Illustrative example: An old routing function approves a flagged request. Before repair, a reviewer derives a rejection expectation from the approved policy and records the failing case. The agent changes the routing condition. The same protected test now passes, while a nearby ordinary request remains covered. A new test that simply copies the agent’s output would not supply that independent challenge.
verification: The original wrong implementation fails a named behavioral assertion.
The corrected candidate passes without an unapproved expectation change.
Boundary and regression checks cover relevant neighboring behavior, with omissions recorded.
outputs: An independently grounded failing case and its post-change result.
A candidate-bound test report with oracle provenance.
risks: Tests generated from a defective implementation can encode its defect as the expected answer.
A maker with write access to the oracle can turn a real failure into a misleading pass.
practice.editorial_note: Editorial operational guidance expanded for Atlas v13.1 from the retained practice descriptor and NDSE2 Chapters 7 and 13 thematic guidance. Family F07 preserves the catalogue classification. The example is illustrative; this entry does not establish measured effectiveness.

records.label: Exploratory Vibe Coding
records.summary: Use conversational generation to explore a design question in a reversible setting. State the hypothesis, permitted effects, and disposal or adoption decision before iterating. A promising prototype can reveal an interaction or feasibility issue, but becoming a maintained product requires a separate decision about ownership, evidence, and operational obligations.
records.limitation: An attractive or apparently complete prototype does not establish maintainability, security, accessibility, or readiness for operational use.

attributes.label: Exploratory Vibe Coding
attributes.required_revision: Keep reversible exploration separate from the decision to adopt its result.
attributes.limitation: An attractive or apparently complete prototype does not establish maintainability, security, accessibility, or readiness for operational use.

practice.purpose: Answer an uncertain design question cheaply enough to discard the experiment when its premise fails.
when_to_use: A team is comparing interaction ideas or testing a narrow technical possibility.
Requirements are provisional and the artifact can remain isolated from consequential users and systems.
when_not_to_use: The work would immediately control sensitive decisions or irreversible effects without an adequate authorized delivery path.
prerequisites: A clear exploratory question, short time budget, and experiment owner.
Disposable data and an environment with bounded effects.
steps: Name the question the prototype should answer and what observation would make it unhelpful.
Set the writable scope, permitted tools, data boundary, and stopping condition before generation.
Iterate on the uncertain aspect; record assumptions and manual shortcuts as they are introduced.
Exercise the relevant interaction or technical path and separate observations from guesses about broader behavior.
Conclude with discard, another bounded experiment, or an explicit adoption proposal that identifies unmet engineering obligations.
practice.example: Illustrative example: A team compares two ways to display policy exceptions using synthetic requests. An assistant generates both interfaces, and the owner observes whether users can distinguish historical and current decisions. The preferred sketch becomes design evidence. Before it enters the maintained service, the team must still review its data model, authorization behavior, accessibility, tests, and ongoing ownership.
verification: The recorded finding answers the original exploratory question.
No prototype shortcut is silently represented as an approved product requirement.
Any proposed adoption names the missing evidence and the responsible decision maker.
outputs: A bounded prototype and an observation log.
A disposal decision or scoped adoption proposal.
risks: Visual polish can encourage premature promotion and hide missing operational behavior.
Repeated exploratory changes can accumulate dependencies that make supposedly disposable work difficult to abandon.
practice.editorial_note: Editorial operational guidance expanded for Atlas v13.1 from the retained practice descriptor and NDSE2 Chapters 1 and 13 thematic guidance. Family F01 preserves the catalogue classification. The example is illustrative; this entry does not establish measured effectiveness.

records.label: Small Verifiable Chunks
records.summary: Divide work into increments whose behavior and impact can be meaningfully checked. A small chunk has one coherent acceptance question, bounded dependencies, and a reviewable result; its size is not determined by line count. Use that semantic scope inside a cycle without assuming that the chunk and the execution cycle are identical concepts.
records.limitation: Artificially tiny edits can obscure a cross-cutting invariant and increase integration work rather than make verification easier.

attributes.label: Small Verifiable Chunks
attributes.required_revision: Small means semantically verifiable; connect it to one-item execution without confusing a chunk with a cycle.
attributes.limitation: Artificially tiny edits can obscure a cross-cutting invariant and increase integration work rather than make verification easier.

practice.purpose: Give a reviewer enough context to diagnose whether a particular intended change has been achieved.
when_to_use: A proposed patch contains multiple unrelated outcomes or failures are difficult to attribute.
An agent needs an item that fits the available evidence, review capacity, and execution budget.
when_not_to_use: Splitting would temporarily violate an invariant that must change atomically across several components.
prerequisites: The intended outcome and affected interfaces are understood.
Relevant checks and required integration obligations are identifiable.
steps: State the behavioral outcome in one sentence and identify what remains explicitly outside the item.
Trace the dependencies required to make that outcome coherent; include necessary files even when this enlarges the diff.
Choose a focused acceptance check and the regressions that protect neighboring obligations.
Implement and inspect the increment as a unit, recording any newly discovered dependency or ambiguity.
Return an independently reviewable result; create a separate item for unrelated findings instead of broadening the current one.
practice.example: Illustrative example: Changing how historical requests are replayed touches a handler, storage adapter, and contract test. Those files belong to one verifiable behavior and stay together. A nearby formatting cleanup and a new reporting endpoint become separate items. If a regression fails, the reviewer can relate it to replay semantics instead of reconstructing three unrelated changes.
verification: The item has one explainable acceptance question and a traceable result.
Its boundaries include the dependencies necessary to preserve the relevant invariant.
The proposed split leaves a viable integration path and records remaining work.
outputs: A scoped work item with acceptance and regression checks.
A reviewable candidate and separate follow-up items.
risks: Using file count as a proxy for simplicity can split behavior across incompatible changes.
Local passes can conceal an integration failure when each chunk is checked in isolation.

Family F03 preserves the catalogue classification. The example is illustrative; this entry does not establish measured effectiveness.
